source_text: Cur autem, licet ad aliam partem disputandi festinare uideamur, illum praetereamus apud apostolum locum? gui cum in forma dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse; sed semetipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accipiens, in similitudine hominum factus, et habitu tnwentus ut homo: humiliauit se, oboediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: propterea et deus illum superexaltauit, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen; ut in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur caelestium terrestrium et infernorum, et omnis lingua confiteatur, quoniam dominus Iesus in gloria est dei patris. qui cum in forma dei esset, inquit. si homo tantummodo Christus, in imagine dei, non forma det rehominem enim scimus ad imaginem, non ad sed nec in angelis formam dei Quis ergo est iste, qui in forma dei, ut diximus, factus est legimus; nisi quoniam hic praecipuus atque generosus prae omnibus dei filius, uerbum dei, imitator omnium paternorum operum, dum et ipse operatur sicut et pater eius, in forma (ut expressimus) est dei patris. et merito in forma pronuntiatus est dei, dum et ipse super omnia, et omnis creaturae diuinam obtinens potestatem, et deus est exemplo patris; hoc ipsum tamen a patre proprio consecutus, ut omnium et deus esset, et dominus esset, et deus ad formam dei patris ex ipso genitus atque prolatus. hic ergo quamuis esset in forma dei, non est rapinam arbitratus aequalem se deo esse. qQuamuis enim se ex deo patre deum esse meminisset, numquam se deo patri aut comparauit aut contulit, memor se esse ex suo patre, et hoc ipsum, quod est, habere se, quia pater dedisset. inde denique et ante carnis assumptionem, sed et post assumptionem corporis, post ipsam praeterea resurrectionem, omnem patri in omnibus rebus oboedientiam praestitit pariter ac praestat. quo probatur numquam arbitratum illum esse rapinam quandam diuinitatem, ut aequaret se patri deo: quin immo contra, omni ipsius imperio et uoluntati oboediens atque subiectus, etiam ut formam serui susciperet contentus fuit—hoc est, hominem illum fieri—et substantiam carnis et corporis, quam ex paternorum secundum hominem delictorum seruitute uenientem nascendo suscepit. quo tempore se etiam exinaniuit, dum humanam condicionis fragilitatem suscipere non recusauit. quoniam si homo tantummodo natus fuisset, per hoc exinanitus non esset. homo enim nascens augetur, non exinanitur: nam dum incipit esse quod cum non esset habere non potuit, ut diximus, non exinanitur, sed potius augetur atque ditatur. at si Christus exinanitur in eo quod nascitur, formam serui accipiendo, quomodo homo tantummodo est? de quo uerius dictum fuisset, locupletatum illum esse tunc cum nasceretur, non exinanitum: nisi quoniam auctoritas diuini uerbi, ad suscipiendum hominem interim conquiescens, nec se suis uiribus exercens, deicit se ad tempus atque deponit, dum hominem fert quem suscepit. exinanit se, dum ad iniurias contumeliasque descendit, dum audit infanda, experitur indigna. cuius tamen humilitatis adest statim egregius fructus. accepit enim omen, quod est super omne nomen, quod utique non aliud intellegimus esse quam nomen dei. nam cum dei sit solius esse super omnia, consequens est, ut nomen illud quod est super omne nomen sit eius, qui super omnia est. dei est ergo nomen illud quod super,omne nomen est: quod nomen est eius utique consequenter, qui, cum in forma dei fuisset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse. neque enim si non deus esset Christus, omne se in nomine eius genu flecteret, caelestium et terrestrium et infernorum: nec uisibilia aut inuisibilia, aut rerum omnium omnis creatura homini esset subiecta siue substrata, quae se ante hominem esse meminisset. ex quo dum iz forma dei esse Christus dicitur, et dum in natiuitatem secundum carnem se exinanisse monstratur, et dum id accepisse nomen a patre quod sit super omne nomen exprimitur, et dum in nomine eius omne genu caelestium, terrenorum et infernorum se flectere et curuare monstratur, et hoc ipsum in gloriam dei patris succurrere asseritur; consequenter non ex illo tantum homo est, quia oboediens patri factus est usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis; sed ex his etiam rebus superioribus diuinitatem Christi sonantibus, dominus Christus Iesus et deus, quod haeretici nolunt, esse monstratur.
pass_a_gloss: But why, although we seem to hasten to another part of the discussion, do we pass over that place in the apostle? Who, when He was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God; but He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man: He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross: therefore God also highly exalted Him, and gave Him a name which is above every name; so that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly and earthly and infernal things, and every tongue should confess, that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. Who, when He was in the form of God, it says. If Christ were only a man, in the image of God, not in the form - for we know that man is according to the image, not according to the form, nor in the angels the form of God - Who then is this, who was made in the form of God, as we have said, we read; unless because this is the chief and noble Son of God above all, the Word of God, imitator of all the paternal works, while He also works just as His Father, in the form (as we have expressed) of God the Father. And rightly He was pronounced in the form of God, while He also is above all, and holds the divine power of all creation, and is God by the example of the Father; this very thing, however, He obtained from the Father, that He might be God of all, and Lord, and God in the form of God the Father, born and brought forth from Him. Therefore, although He was in the form of God, He did not think it robbery to be equal to God. For although He remembered that He was God from God the Father, He never compared or likened Himself to God the Father, mindful that He is from His Father, and that He has this very thing, which He is, because the Father gave it to Him. From this, finally, both before the assumption of flesh and after the assumption of the body, after the resurrection itself, He rendered equal obedience to the Father in all things; by which it is proved that He never thought it robbery to be a certain divinity, so as to equal Himself to God the Father: but rather, on the contrary, obedient and subject to every command and will of His, He was content even to take the form of a servant - that is, to become that man - and the substance of flesh and body, which, born from the servitude of the paternal sins according to man, He undertook. At which time He also emptied Himself, while not refusing to undertake the human condition of fragility. For if He had been born only as a man, He would not have been emptied; for man, being born, grows, is not emptied: for while he begins to be what he was not able to have, as we have said, he is not emptied, but rather grows and is enriched. But if Christ is emptied in being born, taking the form of a servant, how is He only a man? Of whom it would have been more truly said that He was enriched, not emptied, when He was born: unless because the authority of the divine Word, resting to undertake man in the meantime, and not exercising His powers, lowers Himself for a time and lays down, while bearing the man whom He undertook. He empties Himself, while descending to injuries and insults, while hearing infamous things, experiencing unworthy things. Of which humility, however, the excellent fruit is present immediately. For He received the name which is above every name, which we certainly understand to be none other than the name of God. For since it is God's alone to be above all, it follows that the name which is above every name is of Him who is above all. The name, therefore, which is above every name is God's: which name is, of course, consequently of Him, who, when He was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God. For if Christ were not God, every knee would not bow to Him, of heavenly and earthly and infernal things: nor would all creation, visible or invisible, or all things, be subject to man, who remembered that He was before man. From which, while Christ is said to be in the form of God, and while He is shown to have emptied Himself into the birth according to the flesh, and while it is expressed that He received the name from the Father which is above every name, and while it is shown that every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal things bows and curves in His name, and this very thing is asserted to occur in the glory of God the Father; consequently, not only from this is Christ a man, because He was made obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross; but also from these preceding things, which proclaim the divinity of Christ, the Lord Christ Jesus is shown to be God, which the heretics do not want.

pass_b_english: Why, though we appear to be rushing on to another part of the argument, do we skip over that passage in the apostle Paul? He writes of the one who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness; and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death — even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:5-11).

"Who, existing in the form of God," he says. If Christ were merely a man, he would be in the image of God, not in the form — for we know that human beings are made according to the image, not the form, and even angels do not possess the form of God. Who, then, is this one who was found in the form of God, as we have said, unless he is that chief and noble Son of God above all, the Word of God, imitator of all the Father's works, who himself works just as his Father does, and so exists in the form of God the Father (as we have expressed it)? And rightly he is declared to be in the form of God, since he is above all and holds the divine power over all creation, and is God by the example of the Father. Yet this very status he received from the Father, so that he might be God over all, and Lord, and God in the form of God the Father, begotten and brought forth from him.

Therefore, although he existed in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized. For even though he knew himself to be God from God the Father, he never compared or equated himself with God the Father, mindful that he is from his Father and that he possesses his very being because the Father gave it to him. Consequently, both before the assumption of flesh and after the assumption of the body — indeed, even after the resurrection itself — he rendered the same obedience to the Father in all things. By this it is proved that he never regarded his divinity as something to be grasped in order to make himself equal to God the Father; on the contrary, obedient and subject to every command and will of the Father, he was content even to take the form of a servant — that is, to become that man — and to assume the substance of flesh and body, which, born from the bondage of ancestral sins according to human nature, he undertook at his birth. At that time he also emptied himself, because he did not refuse to take on the frailty of the human condition.

If he had been born only as a man, he would not have been emptied; for a human being, when born, grows rather than is emptied. As he begins to be what he could not previously possess, he is not diminished but rather increased and enriched. But if Christ is emptied by being born, by taking the form of a servant, how can he be only a man? Of such a one it would more truly be said that he was enriched, not emptied, at birth — unless the authority of the divine Word, temporarily resting from exercising its powers in order to take on humanity, lowered itself for a time and laid aside its glory, while bearing the man it had assumed. He empties himself as he descends to injuries and insults, as he hears unspeakable things and suffers unworthy treatment. Yet the splendid fruit of that humility appears at once: he received the name that is above every name, which we certainly understand to be nothing other than the name of God (Philippians 2:9-10).

For since it belongs to God alone to be above all, it follows that the name which is above every name belongs to the one who is above all. That name, therefore, is the name of God — and consequently it belongs to the one who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized. For if Christ were not God, every knee would not bow to him — in heaven, on earth, and under the earth — nor would all creation, visible and invisible, be subjected to a mere man who remembered that he existed before humanity. From all this — while Christ is said to be in the form of God, while he is shown to have emptied himself in the birth according to the flesh, while it is declared that he received from the Father the name above every name, while it is shown that every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bows and bends at his name, and that this very thing happens to the glory of God the Father — it follows necessarily that Christ is not a man merely because he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross; but also from these earlier realities that proclaim the divinity of Christ, the Lord Christ Jesus is shown to be God, which the heretics refuse to accept.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments of Novatian regarding the distinction between 'form' (forma) and 'image' (imago), and the nature of Christ's self-emptying (exinanitio). Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source. Scripture citations (Philippians 2:5-11 and 2:9-10) correctly identify the allusions in the text. The translation of 'rapinam' as 'robbery' or 'something to be seized' preserves the author's specific nuance regarding Christ not grasping equality. All clauses, including the subtle distinction between being 'enriched' (augetur) and 'emptied' (exinanitur) during birth, are present.
